🗒️What This Means For You

At trading day 47 (last close) it was +0.87% against a five-campaign average of -1.58% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -1.33%. The 10-year is -8bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 800bp against a five-year average of 423bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +49bp and BB +15bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.35 → 0.68 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+9bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,323bp, -2bp since 2026-11-20, through the Oct 15 record — the market is not buying Nvidia's backstop. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 76.2 (16.2%, -2.2pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 149bp, Oracle 348bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -29%, NBIS -49%, IREN -54% vs NVDA -41%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 34 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -22.1% vs -20.6% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 50% in 3m, 35% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 70%. 6m odds -29.9pp since 2026-11-20. Triggered signposts: CoreWeave 5Y CDS; VXN (Nasdaq vol); Basket names >20% off high; SOX.
  • Stocks: Huge bounce: Nasdaq up 6.5%, S&P up 4.7%, fear gauge sharply lower.
  • FX: Dollar firmer, up about half a percent; euro and yen barely moved.
  • Technicals: Even after today, S&P and Nasdaq still sit below key trend lines.
  • Sectors: Tech led by 9%; energy and staples fell; tech still down 11% this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Weakest junk bonds pay the most extra interest in five years; not easing.

US stocks staged a violent relief rally. The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51% to 24,089.56, the S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17, the Dow rose 3.01% and the Russell 2000 rose 3.40%. The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62 from 35.89. Info Tech jumped 9.03% and Comm Services 5.18%, while Energy (−1.32%) and Staples (−0.09%) lagged. Europe followed more modestly: SX5E +2.23%, STOXX 600 +1.81%. Brent fell 3.34% to $89.48. The 2Y rose 4.69bp to 4.69% while the 10Y was flat at 4.94%. A short-end selloff on a big up day fits a Fed that is still leaning toward hikes. I could not find a verifiable news trigger dated today, so I am not attributing the move to a cause. The story under the headline is credit, which has not confirmed the rally. Bloomberg's HY contagion read (as of Nov 20) has the Caa–B gap at 800bp. That is its 99.8th percentile over five years, against a 5y average of ~423bp, and the widest since 2020-04-15. The stress is spreading up the quality ladder: single-B is +49bp over a month to 374bp, Ba +15bp to 221bp, and IG +9bp to 96bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation rose from 0.35 three months ago to 0.68, just under its 0.69 five-year median. CCC rot is leaking into single-B, BB is starting to move, and IG is only grazed. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. The AI-credit backstop question gets the same answer. CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1,323bp, 128bp above its 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and +152bp over the week, and it barely improved today (−2bp) despite the equity surge. Nvidia CDS is 149bp, +21bp on the week. On this evidence the market is not yet buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds (descriptive). The tech-analog model still places the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), day 34, with the basket −22.1% vs −20.6% for 2000 on the same day. Four signposts are triggered: CoreWeave CDS through its record, VXN 35.91 above 35, 78.6% of basket names more than 20% off their highs, and SOX −34.5% from its 52-week high. The model's 6-month P2+P3 odds fell 29.9pp vs Nov 20. The rally-watch reads 'VIX has spiked but credit is widening': HY is +41bp over 10 days against a ≤+10bp calm test. Sentiment flipped from fear to relief in one session. Positioning should wait for credit to follow.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.27 vol points (5th percentile of the 76 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.9 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 69bp (flatter by 14bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (122bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 53 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Sticky and edging up. The underlying trend measures sit in the upper third of their history and are mostly rising, so inflation is not re-accelerating sharply but is not converging to 2% either. Breadth is two-sided: a large share of the PCE basket is running hot while about a quarter is falling. That argues against a quick Fed pivot and backs the hiking bias.

BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 6 beyond 2000 — 54/100
Today looks less like March-2000 peak froth and more like the early stage of a de-rating. On the froth gauges the computed indicators are far from the 2000 peak. Nasdaq trailing P/E is 38.57x vs 175x (15% of the way), the Nasdaq is −4.3% below its 200DMA (0% of the 2000 stretch), and SOX P/E is 32.79x vs 60x (32%). The catalyst and regime gauges are closer to or past 2000 conditions: IG tightness (120%), Baa–10y tightness (144%), NFCI looseness (151%) and commodities-vs-equities (200%). Easy financial conditions and complacent spreads, not valuation, are the 2000-like part. The phase model puts the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm) at day 34, with the basket −22.1% vs −20.6% for 2000 on the same day. At 6 months the model's odds are P1 39.6%, P2 27.1%, P3 8.0% and P4 25.3%. At 12 months the odds of ever reaching P2+ are 69.9%; these are model estimates, not certainties. Four signposts have triggered (CoreWeave CDS record, VXN >35, breadth, SOX −34.5%). The defensive dial is Step 1, Cautious, since 2026-11-05.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Look-alikes, day 34: NDX −14.3% vs 1997 −10.3%, 1998 −17.8%, 1999 −2.7% and 2000 −25.3%. The closest path is the 1997 Asia episode, a recoverable shock. The Fed then was holding in 1997 and 1998 and hiking in 1999 and 2000; it is hiking now, and 0 of 5 recovery signposts are on. The model's 6-month P2+P3 odds fell 29.9pp vs Nov 20, and the 3-month P2+P3 odds behind the dial are 49.6%, just under the 50% step-down line. The rally-watch shows a VIX spike and turn but fails the credit-calm test. Historically 38.2% of such setups were traps, with typical traps lasting about 9 days for +10.6% before failing, against about 44 days and +31.3% for real rallies. The tilt, per the model, has historically favoured gold, Treasury duration and IG credit over mega-cap growth, developed international and EM. The analyst-estimate inputs are approximate: top-10 S&P weight ~38%, CAPE ~36x, market cap/GDP ~195%, IPO froth ~30/100 (pipeline thin, deals postponed in the fall), long-term EPS-growth expectations ~60/100. 🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December FOMC: a 25bp hike is a live possibility. This is an inference from the record: the October hold at 3.75–4.00% drew three hawkish dissents (9–3) for a quarter-point increase, and JPMorgan pulled its hike call forward to December. Today's 2Y rise is consistent with that. The counter-view (ABN AMRO) saw room to cut. Expect Warsh to give little explicit guidance.

~1 YEAR

Inferred from Warsh's long-standing on-record views, not stated policy. He favours less forward guidance, a smaller balance sheet and institutional reform, including the announced trimmed meeting calendar from 2027 with one meeting skipping a rate vote. Over about a year: rates held at or modestly above current levels while core PCE stays above 3%, with continued balance-sheet restraint. Cuts would likely need a credit/labor break; Sahm is 0.00 and claims 203k, so not yet.

Warsh called the Fed's earlier hike 'serious' and 'responsible' and said politics played no role in decisions. His style keeps the path deliberately vague. With core PCE at 3.12%, sticky CPI near 3.1% and the tech-analog model reading the Fed as 'hiking' (as in 1999/2000, unlike 1997/98), the bias stays hawkish. Spreading HY stress is the main thing that could stay his hand. Near-term and 1-year calls are analyst inference.
